extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax practitioners, employers, payroll and benefits administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Final Treasury/IRS regulations defining what counts as 'qualified tips' under section 224, the reporting and documentation required, limitations on the deduction, and anti-abuse rules; includes examples and special rules (TRDA/GITCA, occupations list, illegal activity exclusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tips (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to paragraph (c) requirements, 'qualified tips' are amounts received as cash tips by an individual in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, as provided in paragraph (h) of this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualified tips are only those cash tips received in eligible occupations (see the List of Occupations that Receive Tips referenced in paragraph (h)). Other statutory and regulatory requirements to claim the deduction under section 224 must also be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cash tips defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Cash tips are tips received, directly or indirectly, from payors, including tips received through mandatory or voluntary tip-sharing arrangements, that are paid in a cash medium of exchange (cash, check, credit/debit card, gift card, tokens readily exchangeable for fixed cash such as casino chips, and other electronic settlement/mobile payment applications denominated in cash). Includes foreign currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cash tips do not include items paid in media other than cash (tickets, meals, services) or digital assets as defined in section 6045(g)(3)(D) and §1.6045‑1(a)(19). Tip-pooling receipts are included as cash tips for recipients except as limited by the managers/supervisors rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tips defined (excess over agreed/expected payment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tips are amounts paid by payors for services that are in excess of the amount agreed to, required, charged, or otherwise reasonably expected to be paid for the services in an arm's-length transaction. Superficial or nominal tokens of appreciation negligible in value do not alter the nature of a payment as a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A payment must be in excess of the agreed/expected charge to be a tip; amounts that are part of the contract price or required access fees are not tips. Examples illustrate contracts, required contributions for access, and token appreciation payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amounts must be paid voluntarily (no compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts are qualified tips only to the extent they are paid voluntarily and without consequence in the event of nonpayment (including any effect on scope or cost of service), are not negotiable, and are determined by the payor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service charges, mandatory automatic gratuities, and any other mandatory amounts automatically added to a customer's bill are not qualified tips even if distributed to employees. Amounts voluntarily paid in excess of mandatory charges may be qualified. The rule is illustrated with multiple POS, contract, and recommended-tip examples (e.g., forced POS selections that require a nonzero tip are not voluntary; tip sliders allowing zero are voluntary; recommended tips with option to modify or zero are voluntary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payor defined
rubrics_metrics.description: For this section, 'payor' means the ultimate recipient of the services (typically the customer, client, or other service recipient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An entity that merely acts as a conduit to remit a tip initially paid by a customer — such as an employer, a third-party settlement organization, or a sole proprietorship/SM‑LLC through which a tip recipient does business — is not the payor for purposes of this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employees in voluntary tip reporting programs (TRDA/GITCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who enter into a Tip Reporting Determination Agreement (TRDA) or a Gaming Industry Tip Compliance Agreement (GITCA) may determine qualified tips using the tip rate in their agreement (and amounts reported on Form 4137) in lieu of reporting actual tips received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of TRDA/GITCA tip rates does not affect tip audit protection under the agreement. Employees remain subject to all other section 224 and regulatory requirements. Examples (gambling dealers) illustrate W-2 reporting at agreed tip rates and ability to claim deduction based on reported amount; employees may instead report full actual tips on Form 4137 to use that amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal activities and other excluded services
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amount received for services the performance of which is a felony or misdemeanor under applicable law is not a qualified tip. Specifically listed exclusions include amounts received for prostitution and pornography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate that even if an occupation appears on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips, tips received while performing illegal services (e.g., unlicensed alcohol service if that is a crime) are not qualified tips for deduction purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managers and supervisors — tip pool receipts not qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received by a manager or supervisor through a voluntary or mandatory tip-sharing arrangement (such as a tip pool) are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, amounts received directly by a supervisor or manager for services they personally provided in the course of duties performed in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips (as provided in paragraph (h)) are qualified tips if all other requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-abuse — recharacterization of wages or payments as tips
rubrics_metrics.description: An amount is not a qualified tip if, based on all relevant facts and circumstances, the amount represents a recharacterization of wages or payments for goods or services as tips for purposes of claiming the deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts/circumstances that may indicate recharacterization include (A) invoice charge less than payment on receipt with tip approximating the difference, and (B) a significant shift in historical tipping or payment practices between payor and tip recipient. The regulation provides examples and tests to identify recharacterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrebuttable presumption of recharacterization (employer payor or ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an irrebuttable presumption that an amount is a recharacterization (and thus not a qualified tip) when (A) the employer of an employee is the payor of a cash tip received by the employee, or (B) the tip recipient has a direct ownership interest in the payor of a cash tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For (B), an ownership interest means (for corporations) ownership of 5% or more of stock; (for partnerships) 5% of profits or capital interest; in other cases, more than 5% beneficial interest. Direct ownership includes ownership held directly or through certain disregarded entities, qualified S sub subsidiaries, grantor trusts, custodians, nominees, etc. Ownership is tested as of the date the tip is received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting/documentation required for qualified tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified tips must be included separately on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), 6041A(e)(3), 6050W(f)(2), or 6051(a)(18) of the Code, or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (Social Security and Medicare Tax on Unreported Tip Income) (or successor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble also notes qualified tips reported on Form W-2 or Form 4137 (and mentions Form 1099‑NEC, Form 1099‑K, and Form 1099‑MISC in context) as bases for claiming the deduction. Examples clarify when self-employed persons must have tips reflected on information returns to deduct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction limitations and AGI-based reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount allowed as a deduction for qualified tips is limited to $25,000 per taxable year (regardless of filing status). After that limit, the allowable amount is further reduced by $100 for each $1,000 (rounded) by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 for joint returns), but not below zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modified adjusted gross income is AGI increased by amounts excluded under sections 911, 931, or 933. The regulation includes numeric examples showing how to apply the $25,000 ceiling and compute the $100 per $1,000 phaseout (illustrative single and joint filer examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation list / mapping to SOC codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility requires that the individual's occupation is among those that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024; occupations are enumerated in the List of Occupations that Receive Tips and mapped via SOC codes using self-reported occupation strings on Form 1040.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains mapping limitations (misspellings, mismatches like 'Student' entered instead of 'bartender') and that mapping shortcomings explain why the table's occupations sum to less than all reported tips. The List gives taxpayers clarity but mapping errors may affect classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cash tips and digital/other media exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cash tips exclude items paid in any medium other than cash (e.g., event tickets, meals, services) and exclude digital assets as defined in section 6045(g)(3)(D) and §1.6045‑1(a)(19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule clarifies that only mediums denominated in cash (including specified electronic payments and foreign currency) count. The preamble example with digital content creators shows required payments for access are service payments (not tips), while additional voluntary contributions beyond required access can be qualified tips if otherwise meeting requirements and properly reported.
